Nos. 26A476 & 26A477
IN THE 
Supreme Court of the United States ______________
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION
Applicant,
v.
SHERROD BROWN, ET AL.
Respondents.
______________
NATIONAL REPUBLICAN CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE, ET AL.
Applicants,
v. 
SHERROD BROWN, ET AL.
Respondents.
______________
ON APPLICATIONS FOR STAY AND ADMINISTRATIVE STAY
PENDING PETITIONS FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI 
______________
RESPONDENTS’ OPPOSITION TO STAY APPLICATIONS
______________
David R. Fox
 Counsel of Record
Nicole E. Wittstein
Julianna D. Astarita
ELIAS LAW GROUP LLP
250 Massachusetts Ave. NW, Suite 400
Washington, DC 20001
(202) 948-1135
dfox@elias.law
Counsel for Respondents Sherrod Brown, Jon Ossoff, 
Roy Cooper, and Kristen McDonald Rivet

1
INTRODUCTION
The question these Applications present is fundamental: may a federal agency 
engage in blatant procedural trench warfare to stave off judicial review of an unlawful 
agency directive until it is too late to matter? Applicants insist that the answer is 
yes—“maybe after ‘nineteen years,’” they say, the Candidates could get a court order 
requiring the Federal Communications Commission to decide their pending 
Application for Review so that judicial review of the pure question of statutory 
construction ultimately at issue in these proceedings can begin. NRCC Appl. 17. 
Meanwhile, the challenged directive remains in effect, the Candidates are up for 
election in just over three weeks, and they are experiencing exactly the deluge of 
party spending at the candidate rate that Republican Party committees promised to 
unleash to “obliterate” them in response to the challenged agency directive.1
The Fourth Circuit was correct to compel the Commission to issue the denial 
of the Candidates’ Application for Review that the Commission has obviously already 
decided to issue, so that judicial review can commence. A Commission decision is 
mandatory: the Communications Act provides that “every such application shall be 
passed upon by the Commission.” 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(4). The Commission does not 
need more time; it is not even required to explain itself. Id. § 155(c)(5). And the 
Commission’s actions in these proceedings make clear that it has been manipulating 
the timing and content of its review procedures to forestall judicial review.
1 Matthew Foldi, INTERVIEW: RNC Chair Joe Gruters on the RNC’s election integrity 
wins and how the GOP can defy history in 2026, Wash. Reporter (June 23, 2026),
https://perma.cc/8Q4T-KLLW.

2
This Court’s stay in NRCC is not to the contrary. NRCC v. Brown, No. 26A274, 
2026 WL 2618462 (U.S. Sep. 4, 2026) (“NRCC”), granting stay pending cert. of 
judgment in Brown v. FCC, No. 26-1785, 2026 WL 2493115 (4th Cir. Aug. 25, 2026)
(“Brown I”). The Court held that the Fourth Circuit likely lacked jurisdiction to 
review the Public Notice before the Commission resolved the Candidates’ Application 
for Review. Id. at *1–2. But the Court also explained that “the Commission is required 
to resolve every application it receives.” Id. And it nowhere suggested that the 
underlying Public Notice was lawful—it did not reach that issue. See id. The 
Candidates therefore commenced this mandamus action the next business day after 
the Court’s order, to eliminate the jurisdictional barrier the Court identified and to 
enable the judicial review that the Communications Act provides.
In arguing otherwise, Applicants cannot decide if the Candidates acted too 
quickly, too slowly, or somehow both. In fact, the Candidates have sought, throughout 
the process, to provide the Commission with as much time to resolve their Application 
for Review as possible without giving up their right to judicial review of the unlawful 
Public Notice before it is too late to matter. To the extent “late-breaking changes” now 
threaten any disorder, neither the Candidates nor the Fourth Circuit are responsible 
for them. People Not Politicians v. Onder, No. 26A388, 2026 WL 2883222, at *2 (U.S. 
Sep. 25, 2026). The Candidates sought expedited Commission review back in April, 
shortly after the Public Notice was issued and well before the onset of the lowest unit 
charge period. It is the Commission that decided not to seek comments on or decide 
the Application for Review until now.

3
The Court should deny the Applications, lift the administrative stay, and 
reinstate the Fourth Circuit’s order requiring the Commission to issue a decision on 
the Candidates’ Application for Review so that judicial review can occur.
STATEMENT
I. The Public Notice and the Application for Review
For decades, Section 315(b)(1) of the Communications Act of 1934 has entitled 
“legally qualified candidate[s] for any public office” who “use . . . any broadcasting 
station” shortly before their elections to do so at “the lowest unit charge of the station 
for the same class and amount of time for the same period.” 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1) (“the 
LUC requirement”). In March of this year, the Federal Communications 
Commission’s Media Bureau issued a “Public Notice” directing that political party 
committees engaged in spending they have coordinated with candidates and joint 
fundraising committees (“JFCs”) with candidate and non-candidate members are also 
entitled to lowest unit charge—the first written guidance the Commission had ever 
provided on the subject. Supp. App. 27–28.2
The Media Bureau issued the Public Notice using authority delegated to it by 
the Commission under Section 155(c) of the Communications Act. See 47 U.S.C. 
§ 155(c)(1) (authorizing delegation); 47 C.F.R. § 0.61(e) (delegation to Media Bureau). 
The Act broadly provides that “[a]ny order, decision, report, or action made or taken 
pursuant to any such delegation” has “the same force and effect” as a Commission 
2 Citations to App. are to the Appendix to the United States’s Application, 
No. 26A476. Citations to Supp. App. are to the Supplemental Appendix that 
accompanies this Response.

4
order, “unless reviewed” by the full Commission. 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(3). It further 
provides that “[a]ny person aggrieved by any such order, decision, report or action 
may file an application for review by the Commission,” and that “every such 
application shall be passed upon by the Commission.” Id. § 155(c)(4). “[T]he 
Commission may grant, in whole or in part, or deny such applications without 
specifying any reasons therefor.” Id. § 155(c)(5). “The filing of an application for 
review” is a “condition precedent to judicial review of any order, decision, report, or 
action made or taken pursuant to a delegation . . . .” Id. § 155(c)(7). Judicial review 
may then be had in the courts of appeals under the Hobbs Act. See 47 U.S.C. § 402(a).
The Public Notice came as a surprise to the Candidates and—it seems—the 
broadcasting industry. Just a few months earlier, the Solicitor General had taken the 
opposite position before this Court, responding to concerns that allowing unlimited 
coordinated party expenditures “threaten[ed] to destabilize the lowest-rate-charge 
system for political advertising,” Br. for Intervenor-Resp’ts at 46–48, NRSC v. FEC, 
No. 24-621 (U.S. filed Sep. 29, 2025), by assuring the Court that the Communications 
Act “require[s] broadcasters to charge low rates for candidate spending, but not for 
party spending—whether coordinated or independent.” Reply Br. of Fed. Resp’ts at 
23, NRSC, No. 24-621 (U.S. filed Oct. 29, 2025) (citing 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)). The 
Solicitor General went on to emphasize that even if the Court allowed unlimited 
coordinated spending, “broadcasters still would not be required to charge parties 
special low rates.” Id. Citing the Solicitor General’s statement, the National 
Association of Broadcasters then advised its broadcaster members that they need not

5
offer lowest unit charge for party-coordinated and JFC advertisements. Supp. App. 
30–32.
On March 30, 2026, however, the Commission’s Media Bureau issued the 
Public Notice directing broadcasters to extend lowest unit charge to “(1) authorized 
committees, including authorized committees that engage in joint fundraising with 
legally qualified candidates for federal office, and (2) [for] advertisements that qualify 
as coordinated expenditures of political parties and legally qualified candidates for 
federal office.” Id. at 27. While the Public Notice purported to “restate previous Media 
Bureau guidance,” id. at 28, both the Media Bureau and the Commission have since 
confirmed that the only past “guidance” on this score consists of “informal oral 
opinions” conveyed to broadcasters by telephone. Id. at 37 n.18; see also Br. for Resp’ts 
at 39 n.10, Brown I, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir. July 20, 2026), ECF. No. 49.
On April 29, 2026, the Candidates timely filed an Application for Review 
asking the Commission to set aside the Public Notice. Supp. App. 1–32. On the same 
day, the Television Bureau of Advertising, Inc. (“TVB”)—a broadcaster interest 
group—filed a separate petition for reconsideration before the Media Bureau making 
similar arguments. See Supp. App. 35 & n.1. The Candidates’ Application explained 
that the Public Notice is unlawful because it purports to require stations to offer 
lowest unit charge for advertisements that do not constitute candidate use, in 
violation of Section 315(b)(1)’s plain text. The Candidates twice requested expedited 
relief due to the imminent harm they faced from the Public Notice’s unlawful

6
expansion of lowest unit charge to non-candidate advertising. Supp. App. 4, 24. But 
for months, the Commission did nothing.
II. Brown I and NRCC
With the start of the lowest unit charge period for the general election fast 
approaching, the Candidates filed a Petition for Review of the Public Notice in the 
Fourth Circuit on June 19, 2026. The Fourth Circuit expedited the case to enable a 
decision before lowest unit charge became available on September 4. In its brief and 
at argument, the Commission defended the challenged Public Notice on the merits, 
arguing that it “is entirely consistent with Section 315(b)” of the Communications 
Act. Br. for Resp’ts at 36, Brown I, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir. July 20, 2026), ECF No. 49.
The Commission also suggested that mandamus would have been a more appropriate 
mechanism for the Candidates to obtain relief. Id. at 28. 
The Fourth Circuit heard oral argument in Brown I at a special sitting on 
August 7, 2026. By then, the Candidates’ Application for Review had been pending 
before the Commission for more than three months. But when pressed by the panel, 
the Commission’s counsel admitted with “commendable candor” that “it [was] very 
unlikely that the Commission [would] act” on the Application before lowest unit 
charge became available on September 4, Brown I, 2026 WL 2493115, at *6 (quoting 
C.A. Oral Arg. 49:49–50:12 (Aug. 7, 2026))—even though the Commission had already 
authorized the filing of a brief rejecting the legal basis for the Candidates’ Application 
on the merits, and even though the Commission would have been entitled to deny the 
Application “without specifying any reasons therefor,” 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(5).

7
Just ten days later, however—after an oral argument at which a panel majority 
seemed inclined to grant relief—the Commission changed course. It filed a notice of 
supplemental authority informing the panel that (1) the Media Bureau had issued an 
order denying TVB’s petition for reconsideration of the Public Notice; and (2) “the 
FCC Chairman circulated a proposed order” on the Candidates’ Application for 
Review “dismiss[ing] the application as an improper vehicle” to review the Public 
Notice in the first place. Supp. App. 33. 
On August 25, 2026, before any such order was issued, the Fourth Circuit ruled 
for the Candidates and set aside the Public Notice. The court found that the “unusual 
circumstances” of the case supported the conclusion that the Commission had 
constructively denied the Candidates’ Application for Review, thereby conferring 
jurisdiction to review the Public Notice. Brown I, 2026 WL 2493115, at *6. The court 
then held on the merits that the Public Notice conflicted with the plain text of the 
Communications Act by extending the valuable entitlement to lowest unit charge that 
Congress reserved for federal candidates to non-candidate political committees, 
including party committees and JFCs. Id. at *8–11.
Ten days later, this Court granted an application by the Party Committees and 
stayed the Fourth Circuit’s judgment on procedural grounds. The Court held that the 
Fourth Circuit “likely lacked statutory jurisdiction” because the Commission had not 
yet ruled on the Candidates’ Application for Review. NRCC, 2026 WL 2618462, at *2. 
This Court further held that the Party Committees would face irreparable harm if 
they were required to pay ordinary rates for their advertisements. Id. The Court did

8
not reach the merits of the Candidates’ challenge to the Public Notice, and it did not 
balance the equities between the Party Committees’ injuries and the Candidates’. See 
id.
III. The Present Mandamus Proceeding
On September 8, 2026—the next business day after the Court’s order in 
NRCC—the Candidates filed this mandamus action, which asked the Fourth Circuit 
to order the Commission to issue a decision on their still-pending Application for 
Review. See Mandamus App., In re Brown, No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Sep. 8, 2026), ECF 
No. 2 (the “Mandamus Petition”). The Fourth Circuit ordered the Commission to 
respond by September 15. See Order, In re Brown, No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Sep. 9, 2026), 
ECF No. 12.
On September 15, more than four months after the Candidates filed their 
Application for Review—but mere hours before the Commission’s mandamus 
response was due—the Commission issued a public notice seeking comment on the 
Candidates’ Application, with an expedited comment period closing on September 29, 
2026. The Commission then submitted its response to the Fourth Circuit, arguing 
that mandamus was inappropriate while the “agency process remains ongoing,” and 
asking the court to defer action until it was complete. FCC Resp. at 3, In re Brown, 
No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Sep. 15, 2026), ECF No. 21 (internal quotation marks omitted). 
The Fourth Circuit “accorded grace to the FCC and deferred action on the Mandamus 
Petition until at least October 1, 2026.” App. 13a.
On October 1, the Commission then informed the Fourth Circuit that it had 
opened another new comment period, this one on the broadcast industry’s related

9
application for review, which TVB had filed two weeks earlier on September 14—the 
day before the Commission had asked for comments on the Candidates’ Application. 
This new comment period would extend from September 30 to October 19. The 
Commission therefore asked the Fourth Circuit to delay its mandamus proceedings 
even longer. FCC 28(j) Letter at 2, In re Brown, No. 26-2230 (4th Cir. Oct. 1, 2026), 
ECF No. 28. And the Fourth Circuit waited another six days. But on October 7, it 
announced that its “willingness to tolerate the FCC’s delay tactics [wa]s at an end.” 
App. 15a. Explaining that more than five months had passed since the Candidates 
filed their Application for Review and nearly two months had passed since the 
Chairman circulated a proposed order disposing of the Application, the court rejected 
the Commission’s invocation of “one excuse after another for further delay.” Id. at 18a 
n.2. The Fourth Circuit issued a writ of mandamus ordering the FCC to take action 
on the Candidates’ Application by noon on October 9. Id. at 19a. The Commission and 
the Party Committees responded by seeking a stay from this Court.
LEGAL STANDARD
A stay pending certiorari is an “extraordinary” remedy. Williams v. Zbaraz, 
442 U.S. 1309, 1311 (1979) (Stevens, J., in chambers) (citation omitted). “[A]n 
applicant must show (1) a reasonable probability that four Justices will consider the 
issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair prospect that a majority of 
the Court will vote to reverse the judgment below; and (3) a likelihood that 
irreparable harm will result from the denial of a stay.” Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 
U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). In close cases, the Court “balance[s] the equities 
and weigh[s] the relative harms to the applicant and to the respondent.” Id.

10
ARGUMENT
I. The Fourth Circuit’s order is consistent with this Court’s stay order 
in NRCC.
The Fourth Circuit’s grant of mandamus is entirely consistent with this 
Court’s stay order in NRCC. The Court held in NRCC that “the Fourth Circuit likely 
lacked statutory jurisdiction to address [the Candidates’] challenge” because the 
Commission had not yet resolved their Application for Review. NRCC, 2026 WL 
2618462, at *2. The Court further held that the Party Committees faced irreparable 
harm without a stay. Id. The Party Committees wrongly suggest that the Court 
conducted a balancing of the equities, NRCC Appl. 11, but the Court did no such 
thing. See NRCC, 2026 WL 2618462, at *2. Nor did the Court reach the merits or say 
anything about whether the challenged Public Notice is lawful or must remain in 
effect for the 2026 election. See id. Judge Wilkinson’s insistence that the NRCC stay 
“embraced . . . the need to preserve settled understandings prior to an election,” App. 
25a (Wilkinson, J., dissenting), reads into this Court’s stay order a basis for it that 
simply is not there. 
The Candidates acted quickly, on the next business day after this Court’s 
decision, to attempt to resolve the jurisdictional concern that was the exclusive basis 
for the Court’s order by commencing this mandamus proceeding. Notably, in 
defending against the Candidates’ Petition for Review, even the Commission had 
suggested that mandamus would have been a more appropriate mechanism for the 
Candidates to obtain relief. Br. for Resp’ts at 28, Brown I, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir. July 
20, 2026), ECF No. 49. This proceeding, and the Fourth Circuit’s mandamus order,

11
accept and address the Court’s ruling that judicial review likely must await a 
Commission decision. “[R]equiring the Commission to decide the application does not 
evade the prerequisite [this] Court identified. It requires the Commission to fulfill it.” 
App. 21a (Wynn, J., concurring). 
To the extent there is now uncertainty over the scope of lowest unit charge, 
judicial review is the solution, not the problem. The question involves the scope of a 
statutory right, and only the federal courts can provide an authoritative answer to 
that question. Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 398–401 (2024). The 
Commission cannot change the meaning of the Communications Act from the “single, 
best meaning” that has been “fixed [since] the time of enactment.” Id. at 400 (citation 
omitted). Given that the Commission “literally ha[d] no power to act” to extend lowest 
unit charge beyond its statutory authority, La. Pub. Serv. Comm’n v. FCC, 476 U.S. 
355, 374 (1986), the sooner judicial review occurs, the better—for everyone involved, 
and regardless of the outcome. Only then will the Commission and regulated parties 
know with certainty who is entitled to lowest unit charge and be able to conform their 
conduct accordingly. 
To be sure, the Candidates, too, wish that this question had been answered 
months ago. That is why they sought expedited review by the Commission back in 
April, shortly after the Public Notice was issued, and that is why they filed a Petition 
for Review in the Fourth Circuit in June—after waiting as long as they could to let 
the Commission act, but grounded in what they believed in good faith was the best 
reading of the Communications Act’s judicial review provisions. It is the Commission

12
that has, time and again, “dragg[ed] its feet” and changed its procedural plans to fit 
whatever seemed, at any given time, most likely to ward off judicial review. See App.
1a, 4a–9a, 11a–14a (detailing the procedural history supporting this conclusion). If 
review now occurs on the eve of the election, the Candidates are “not responsible for 
the late-breaking change[].” People Not Politicians, 2026 WL 2883222, at *2. 
II. The Court is unlikely to grant certiorari and reverse.
A. The Fourth Circuit’s discretionary writ is a poor candidate for 
certiorari.
Stripped of their threshold argument that the stay order in NRCC compels the 
same relief here, Applicants offer nothing to support “a discretionary judgment” that 
“the Court should grant review in the case” down the road. Does 1–3 v. Mills, 142 S. 
Ct. 17, 18 (2021) (mem.) (Barrett, J., concurring in denial of application for injunctive 
relief); see also Labrador v. Poe, 144 S. Ct. 921, 931 (2024) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring 
in the grant of stay) (“If the underlying merits issue would not warrant this Court’s 
review when the case returned to the Court on the merits docket, then we should 
deny the application and leave the question of interim relief to the court of appeals.”). 
Unlike in NRCC, there is not even a hint of a circuit split on any question of law; only 
a discretionary determination that under the particular circumstances of this timesensitive case, the Commission’s five-month delay in resolving the Candidates’ 
Application for Review is too long. Applicants cannot “use the emergency docket to 
force the Court to give a merits preview in cases that it would be unlikely to take—
and to do so . . . without benefit of full briefing and oral argument.” Does 1–3, 142 S.
Ct. at 18. Yet that is precisely what Applicants seek here.

13
Certiorari here would be unprecedented. Applicants do not cite, and the 
Candidates have been unable to locate, any case where this Court has granted 
certiorari to review a lower court’s equitable finding that an agency had unlawfully 
delayed taking a discrete action it is required to take—in either a mandamus or 
Administrative Procedure Act posture. That is not surprising. The Court’s review in
such a case would be limited to the extraordinarily fact-bound question of whether 
the court below abused its discretion in finding the agency’s delay unreasonable. See 
Am. Hosp. Ass’n v. Burwell, 812 F.3d 183, 190 (D.C. Cir. 2016) (“[T]hreshold 
requirements for mandamus jurisdiction” are reviewed “de novo,” but the court would 
“review ‘the equities’ for abuse of discretion.”); Hinkel v. England, 349 F.3d 162, 163 
(3d Cir. 2003) (“We generally review mandamus decisions for abuse of discretion.”).
The abuse-of-discretion standard “is limited and deferential,” and the Court 
will affirm so long as the lower court “appl[ied] the correct legal standard and offer[ed] 
substantial justification for its conclusion.” BLOM Bank SAL v. Honickman, 605 U.S. 
204, 216 (2025) (cleaned up). This Court generally does not take up cases “when the 
petitioner claims only that a concededly correct view of the law was incorrectly 
applied to the facts.” Kyles v. Whitley, 514 U.S. 419, 456 (1995) (Scalia, J., dissenting); 
see also Sup. Ct. R. 10 (“A petition for a writ of certiorari is rarely granted when the 
asserted error consists of erroneous factual findings or the misapplication of a 
properly stated rule of law.”). There is no reason it would take up this case under that 
test.

14
B. Mandamus was proper to protect the Fourth Circuit’s future 
jurisdiction.
Perhaps recognizing the unlikelihood that the Court would grant certiorari to 
review a discretionary, equitable finding of unreasonable delay, the Party 
Committees (but not the United States) launch a threshold attack on the Fourth 
Circuit’s mandamus jurisdiction. Mandamus jurisdiction is lacking, they say, because 
the Fourth Circuit’s order “neither preserves existing jurisdiction nor protects future 
jurisdiction.” NRCC Appl. 12. But here it is the Party Committees who ignore NRCC. 
The Fourth Circuit likely lacked jurisdiction, this Court said, because the 
Communications Act requires the Commission to resolve a party’s application for 
review before judicial review may be had. NRCC, 2026 WL 2618462, at *1–2. In 
ordering the Commission to resolve the Candidates’ Application for Review, the 
Fourth Circuit commanded precisely the jurisdictional ingredient that this Court 
held it presently lacks. And to the extent that the Party Committees’ argument is 
that the underlying Public Notice could never be judicially reviewable, NRCC Appl. 
13, that argument is irreconcilable with the Communications Act’s text, see 47 U.S.C. 
§ 155(c)(7) (providing for judicial review of delegated actions at least once the 
Commission resolves an application for review), and with their own representations—
not to mention this Court’s holding in NRCC—that the Public Notice in question was 
so potent that its vacatur irreparably harmed the Party Committees by causing 
broadcasters to rescind favorable rates. See NRCC, 2026 WL 2618462, at *2; see also, 
e.g., Nat’l Env’t Dev. Ass’n’s Clean Air Project v. EPA, 752 F.3d 999, 1007 (D.C. Cir. 
2014) (“If an agency action announces a binding change in its enforcement policy

15
which immediately affects the rights and obligations of regulated parties, then the 
action is likely final and subject to review.”).
C. The Candidates had a clear and indisputable right to a timely 
Commission decision. 
The Fourth Circuit correctly determined the Commission has a “clear duty to 
act” on the Candidates’ Application for Review, as the mandamus standard requires. 
Lovitky v. Trump, 949 F.3d 753, 760 (D.C. Cir. 2020). Agency inaction is cause for 
mandamus relief when the agency has “failed to take a discrete agency action that it 
is required to take.” Norton v. S. Utah Wilderness All., 542 U.S. 55, 64 (2004). Courts 
assess this requirement by “look[ing] to the statutory requirements imposed by 
Congress and whether an Executive Branch agency retains discretion over a 
particular action.” In re Nat’l Nurses United, 47 F.4th 746, 752 (D.C. Cir. 2022). 
1. Applicants do not dispute the Commission’s “clear duty to act” on the 
Candidates’ Application for Review. Nor can they. The Communications Act provides 
that “every such application [for review] shall be passed upon by the Commission.” 47 
U.S.C. § 155(c)(4) (emphasis added). And this Court emphasized in NRCC that “[t]he 
Commission is required to resolve every application it receives.” NRCC, 2026 WL 
2618462, at *1. 
Instead, the Party Committees fault the Fourth Circuit for finding the 
Commission had “a ‘clear duty to act’ on the [Candidates’] application for review by 
October 9,” maintaining the court lacked authority to compel Commission action “by 
a particular date.” NRCC Appl. 14, 16. That argument ignores that unlawful-delay 
claims exclusively arise in the absence of a specific, mandatory statutory deadline.

16
See, e.g., Barrios Garcia v. U.S. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., 25 F.4th 430, 453–54 (6th 
Cir. 2022) (distinguishing claims for agency action unlawfully withheld versus 
unreasonably delayed on this basis); South Carolina v. United States, 907 F.3d 742, 
756 (4th Cir. 2018) (same); Forest Guardians v. Babbitt, 174 F.3d 1178, 1190 (10th 
Cir. 1999) (same). In such cases, courts routinely exercise equitable discretion to 
determine whether an agency’s delay is unreasonable in the circumstances. See 
Telecomms. Rsch. & Action Ctr. v. FCC, 750 F.2d 70, 80 (D.C. Cir. 1984). An order 
requiring the agency to act by a date certain is the ordinary remedy once a court has 
determined delay is unreasonable. See South Carolina, 907 F.3d at 765 (courts 
“retain[] discretion to order agency compliance, including by fixing firm deadlines if 
appropriate, . . . to ensure that the delinquent agency makes serious, vigorous 
attempts to fulfill its statutory responsibilities” (internal quotation marks omitted)).3
Accepting the Party Committees’ position would be a sea change to this wellestablished doctrine. 
Along similar lines, the United States contends that “the statute’s silence on 
timing” means “the Commission retains the freedom to formulate its own procedures 
for how long to take in acting on the application.” U.S. Appl. 9. But therein lies the 
problem: the Commission has not developed general procedures to govern 
applications for review like the Candidates’. “[T]he time agencies take to make 
3 See, e.g., In re A Cmty. Voice, 878 F.3d 779, 788 (9th Cir. 2017) (requiring action 90 
days after decision); In re Core Commc’ns, Inc., 531 F.3d 849, 862 (D.C. Cir. 2008)
(granting writ of mandamus and directing action “by November 5, 2008”); In re Am. 
Rivers & Idaho Rivers United, 372 F.3d 413, 420 (D.C. Cir. 2004) (directing “judicially 
reviewable response” to petition “within 45 days”).

17
decisions must be governed by a ‘rule of reason.’” In re United Mine Workers, 190 F.3d 
545, 549 (D.C. Cir. 1999) (emphasis added). The United States does not identify one; 
the Commission’s shifting approach to the Candidates’ Application based on its 
perceived risk of adverse judicial review belies the existence of any such rule; and the 
Party Committees affirmatively argue that the three-month objective in 47 U.S.C. 
§ 155(d) excludes applications for review, NRCC Appl. 14–15. “A delay in adjudication 
caused by the agency’s failure to follow any rule of reason is, almost tautologically, 
unreasonable.” Jingjing Liu v. Mayorkas, No. 20-cv-654, 2021 WL 2115209, at *3 
(D.D.C. May 25, 2021).
2. Under this well-established doctrine, and in the unique circumstances of 
this case, the Fourth Circuit did not abuse its discretion in finding the Commission’s 
delay in resolving the Candidates’ Application for Review unreasonable. “There is no 
per se rule as to how long is too long to wait for agency action, . . . but a reasonable 
time for agency action is typically counted in weeks or months.” In re Am. Rivers & 
Idaho Rivers United, 372 F.3d at 419 (internal quotation marks omitted). Although 
delays of this length may not typically trigger mandamus relief, as Judge Wilkinson 
acknowledged in Brown I, “courts may calibrate their discretion to issue the writ and 
act more aggressively when the circumstances warrant it.” Brown I, 2026 WL 
2493115, at *20 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). And this is an unusual case. 
To start, as this Court’s NRCC order recognized, the electoral context means 
that this dispute implicates “First Amendment rights to speak” and “reach the 
electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the midterms” that “cannot be remedied

18
after the fact through refunds or reimbursements.” NRCC, 2026 WL 2618462, at *2. 
Moreover, whereas agencies may often need time to make up their minds and prepare 
a reasoned decision, here the Commission’s forceful defense of the Public Notice in 
court leaves no doubt as to its position on the merits, and it is not required to provide 
any reasoning at all, see 47 U.S.C. § 155(c)(5). The issue involves a pure question of 
statutory construction in which the Commission has no particular expertise and 
which will be subject to de novo judicial review in any event. Loper Bright, 603 U.S. 
at 400–01. 
Add to all of that the Commission’s extraordinary procedural acrobatics in this 
matter: months of inaction and a statement at argument that nothing was planned 
any time soon, followed by an abrupt promise of an imminent denial that never came, 
followed by a sudden solicitation of comments on the day the mandamus response

SUMMARY
In 1971, to address candidates’ ballooning campaign costs, Congress required broadcast 
stations to provide special low rates—known as “lowest unit charge”—to candidates in the run-up 
to elections. The plain text of the resulting statute, codified at Section 315(b) of the 
Communications Act, reflects this limited purpose—it entitles only “candidates” to the special 
rates. 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1). But the Media Bureau recently issued guidance purporting to require 
broadcast stations to offer lowest unit charge to advertising purchased by two categories of noncandidate political committees: (1) party committees engaged in coordinated expenditures and (2) 
“Joint Fundraising Committees” (JFCs) with candidate and non-candidate committee members. 
That guidance directly conflicts with the plain text of the Communications Act and the 
Commission should set it aside, making clear that only candidates and candidate committees are 
entitled to lowest unit charge. 
Advertisements by party committees are not entitled to lowest unit charge because they are 
not “use” of a broadcasting station “by . . . a legally qualified candidate,” id., even if they are 
“coordinated” with a candidate. The Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) distinguishes 
between (1) party committee contributions to candidate committees for the candidate’s own use, 
see 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a)(1)(A), (h), and (2) party committee coordinated expenditures, which 
must be made directly by the party committee, see id. § 30116(d). The latter are “use” by a party 
committee, not by a candidate, because they are required to be the party committee’s 
expenditures—if they were the candidate’s use, they would be unlawful contributions to the 
candidate’s committee. 
Advertisements by JFCs with candidate and non-candidate members are also not entitled 
to lowest unit charge because, by law, much of the cost of those advertisements is borne by noncandidate members who are not entitled to lowest unit charge. See 11 C.F.R. § 102.17(c)(7). The

Media Bureau justified its guidance by noting that JFCs can be formally designated as “authorized 
committees” of candidates under FECA. But FECA allows candidates to designate JFCs as 
“authorized committees” “solely for the purpose of joint fundraising.” 52 U.S.C. 
§ 30102(e)(3)(A)(ii) (emphasis added). That designation reflects that the JFC spends the
candidate’s share of fundraising expenses and receives the candidate’s share of contributions on 
behalf of the candidate, before transferring the candidate’s share of net proceeds to the candidate’s 
principal committee. See id. § 30101(6). It does not justify treating JFC expenditures as candidate 
expenditures entitled to lowest unit charge, even though some, and often nearly all, of those 
expenditures are paid for by non-candidate committees with no right to lowest unit charge.

BACKGROUND
I. Statutory and regulatory framework
A. The “lowest unit charge” entitlement
Section 315(b)(1) of the Communications Act of 1934 entitles “legally qualified 
candidate[s] for any public office” who “use . . . any broadcasting station” shortly before their 
elections to do so at “the lowest unit charge of the station for the same class and amount of time 
for the same period.” 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1). This valuable entitlement takes effect 45 days before 
the candidate’s primary election or runoff and 60 days before the candidate’s general election. Id.
§ 315(b)(1)(A). It was enacted in its present form as part of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 
1971 (FECA), which comprehensively regulates the finances of federal campaigns. See Hernstadt 
v. FCC, 677 F.2d 893, 897 (D.C. Cir. 1980). 
FECA requires all federal candidates to designate a “principal campaign committee” to 
accept contributions and make expenditures on their behalf. 52 U.S.C. § 30102(e)(1). Everyone 
agrees that stations must offer lowest unit charge for advertisements purchased by those principal 
campaign committees on behalf of the “legally qualified candidate” they support. This Application 
concerns whether stations must also offer lowest unit charge to advertisements purchased by two 
other categories of committees that are further removed from the candidates themselves: party 
committees engaged in coordinated expenditures under 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d), and joint fundraising 
committees established by candidates and non-candidates “solely for the purpose of joint 
fundraising by such candidates,” id. § 30102(e)(3)(A)(ii). While the dispute is ultimately over the 
meaning of the Communications Act, understanding it requires an explanation of federal campaign 
finance law’s treatment of those two categories of committees.
Party Committee Coordinated Expenditures. FECA sharply limits the size of 
“contributions” that may be made to federal political committees, including candidate committees.

Many stations have encountered independent entities such as political action 
committees (PACs) or political parties, claiming to be “authorized” by a candidate and 
thus entitled to the “lowest unit charge” (LUC) for political advertising under Section 
315(b) of the Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. § 315(b)). This question has also 
arisen in related litigation currently pending before the U.S. Supreme Court. This memo 
presents NAB staff’s view of whether such claims, as a general matter, may be valid. 
This memo is not intended to provide legal advice on how the law or legal principles 
discussed herein may apply to a broadcast station’s specific circumstances. Indeed, 
each station faces its own unique political and economic environment, and as such, the 
applicability of these views will vary based on the situation. Stations should seek the 
advice of their own attorneys when deciding whether an advertisement qualifies for the 
LUC.
NAB believes that, while a candidate’s “authorized committee” is entitled to LUC, other 
entities are not. Specifically, under the applicable federal laws, a candidate’s designated 
principal campaign committee is entitled to LUC rates, while “joint fundraising 
committees” and other “hybrid” committees are not. In fact, as detailed below, the 
Department of Justice, through the Solicitor General, recently reflected a similar view.
Although Section 315(b) only mentions LUC in the context of candidate ads, the FCC 
has historically interpreted the law to apply to both a “legally qualified candidate” and 
the “authorized committee of such candidate.” Section 315(b)(2) states that an ad by a 
candidate and any “authorized committee” of the candidate that references an opponent 
for the same office is only entitled to the LUC if the ad includes the “stand by your ad” 
statement that the candidate has approved the ad. In a 1972 Public Notice, for instance, 
the FCC specifically denied that the LUC provision of Section 315(b)(1) applied to 
political broadcasts by groups, organizations, or persons other than candidates, stating: 
“The provision applies only to broadcasts by candidates for public office.” Similarly, in a
1992 Memorandum Opinion and Order codifying its prior political programming policies, 
the FCC stated: “[W]e have always held that only candidates or their authorized 
campaign committees are entitled to the LUC pursuant to Section 315(b). Thus, even if 
an independent entity produces an advertisement that includes an appearance by a 
candidate, that independent entity is not entitled to the LUC.” Accordingly, it is not 
sufficient for candidate to “authorize” or approve any particular advertisement. For any

Nothing about this proceeding was handled correctly. The Media Bureau, without seeking 
comment, released a public notice purporting to restate existing legal authority.7 The Order on 
Reconsideration characterizes the LUC PN as merely restating existing legal authority and, on 
that basis, dismisses the substantive challenges as procedurally defective.8 There is, however, no 
citation to a substantive Commission action as a source of the “rule” at issue. Instead, there is a 
citation to a rule providing that broadcasters may seek an oral opinion or ruling from staff.9
Based on the allowed practice that provides a means for individual entities to seek guidance on 
specific facts, the Media Bureau asserts that unwritten informal guidance provided by Media 
Bureau staff at some unidentified point in the past created “existing legal authority” about which 
the LUC PN is merely reminding broadcasters.10 The LUC PN relies on such informal guidance 
and then the Order on Reconsideration relies on the LUC PN. “Existing legal authority” cannot 
lawfully be created out of thin air in this manner. 
The substantive precedent on which the Commission relies for the interpretation and application 
of complex interrelated statutes is unwritten informal guidance. While an individual broadcaster 
or its customer may be allowed to rely on unwritten informal guidance in its individual actions, 
this unwritten informal guidance is being treated here as an established generally applicable rule. 
Even setting aside the wholesale lack of notice and comment and final appealable order 
published in the Federal Register, the Media Bureau does not have the authority to adopt 
generally applicable rules because such action would be new and novel and outside of its 
delegated authority.11

Significant legal issues were raised in both the Petition for Reconsideration and the Application 
for Review that were not adequately addressed, if at all, in the Order on Reconsideration. These 
include, but are not limited to, a complex analysis of the distinctions between sections (b)(1) and 
(b)(2) of 47 U.S.C. § 315,12 serious questions about whether the expanded interpretation violates 
either the First Amendment or the Takings Clause of the Constitution,13 and the contradiction 
between the LUC PN and the U.S. Solicitor General’s statement to the Supreme Court that the 
Communications Act “require[s] broadcasters to charge low rates for candidate spending, but not 
for party spending—whether coordinated or independent.”14 Again, the Media Bureau did not 
seek comment on these questions. 
The Order on Reconsideration asserts further that there are adequate processes available for 
parties to challenge the substance of the LUC PN because any specific disputes can be 
adjudicated on a case-by-case basis.15 This assertion ignores the very time-sensitive and serious 
facts before us in this case. The 60-day window at issue opens next week. This 60-day window is 
critical to both broadcasters and candidates for distinct reasons that are reflected in their filings.16
The process identified by the Media Bureau will not address the issues raised in a timely manner.
